Resource Nationalism for the 21st Century: Why America Must Prioritize Its Own

An OWL Analysis

Introduction

The United States of America possesses a remarkable endowment of natural resources — from the vast freshwater reserves of the Great Lakes to the rich deposits of rare earth minerals dotting the Mountain West, from the energy shale formations stretching beneath Appalachia to the oil reserves of the Permian Basin. For decades, America has operated under a paradigm of open markets, globalized supply chains, and comparative advantage — the idea that free trade in natural resources benefits all parties. Yet this paradigm is fraying, and with frightening speed. In an era of rising geopolitical competition with resource-hungry adversaries, accelerating climate vulnerabilities, and fragile global supply chains, the United States must fundamentally reorient its resource policies inward. It must adopt robust resource nationalism — the deliberate prioritization of domestic needs in water, energy, and critical minerals — including the severe restriction or outright ban on their export.

This is not a call born of xenophobia or economic ignorance. It is a call rooted in national security imperatives, long-term economic strategy, environmental stewardship, and a sober assessment of a world that is becoming less cooperative and more zero-sum. The argument for resource nationalism is, ultimately, an argument for survival and sovereignty.

I. National Security Demands Resource Independence

The most urgent and unassailable argument for resource nationalism is national security. No responsible nation ships the very materials that undergird its military superiority and industrial capacity to strategic adversaries without serious restriction.

The Rare Earth Minerals Crisis

Rare earth elements — including neodymium, dysprosium, lithium, cobalt, and others — are the backbone of modern defense technology. They are essential for manufacturing precision-guided missiles, stealth aircraft components, advanced radar systems, night-vision equipment, jet engines, and the guidance systems that make American military technology the most sophisticated on Earth.

Yet the United States imports approximately 80% of its rare earth minerals from China, and Chinese companies control a dominant share of global processing capacity. This is not a mere trade imbalance; it is a strategic chokehold that Beijing has explicitly demonstrated willingness to exploit. In 2010, China cut off rare earth exports to Japan during a territorial dispute. President Xi Jinping has visited rare earth processing facilities with thinly veiled threats. The 2019 Chinese state media discussion of weaponizing rare earth exports during the trade war was not hypothetical posturing — it was a preview.

By continuing to export domestically mined rare earths and critical minerals to any nation, particularly strategic competitors, the United States is actively subsidizing the military-industrial capacity of countries that are actively developing weapons systems intended to counter American superiority. Every ton of unprocessed lithium or rare earth concentrate shipped overseas is potentially a ton that will be refined, engineered, and integrated into an adversary's weapons platform. The moral and strategic absurdity of this arrangement cannot be overstated.

Resource nationalism in this context is not protectionism — it is common sense. The United States restricts the export of advanced semiconductor technology through the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security. It maintains a strict arms embargo against certain nations. The logic is identical: critical materials that underpin defense capabilities must be conserved and controlled.

Energy Independence as Security Imperative

America's energy security is equally vulnerable. While the shale revolution has made the United States a net energy exporter in certain categories, the infrastructure and policy framework still treat energy as a freely traded commodity rather than an asset of last resort. Energy nationalism would mandate strategic reserves far beyond the current Strategic Petroleum Reserve, encourage domestic consumption of American-produced energy at preferential prices, and restrict exports during times of international or domestic crisis.

The lessons of the 1970s oil embargo, of Europe's dependence on Russian natural gas (a dependence that enriched Putin's war machine for decades), and of recent global energy price shocks all converge on a single conclusion: nations that depend on global markets for energy supply are nations that can be coerced. America must produce energy for Americans first, and treat surplus as a geopolitical tool — not a profit center to be indiscriminately sold to the highest bidder.

II. Economic Sovereignty Requires Resource Control

Beyond security, the economic case for resource nationalism is powerful and multi-dimensional.

Capturing Full Value Through Domestic Processing

One of the most egregious failures of current policy is the export of raw, unprocessed natural resources. The United States mines rare earths at Mountain Pass, California, yet ships much of the concentrate to China for processing. The same pattern applies to lithium, copper, timber, and other resources. The result is that America captures only a fraction of the total value chain — the low-value extraction stage — while exporting the high-value manufacturing, processing, and refining stages to foreign nations, including adversaries.

Resource nationalism would reverse this by tying resource access to domestic processing. If you wish to extract American minerals, you will build American processing facilities, employ American workers, and pay American taxes. This is not novel — it is the model that built the American industrial base in the 19th century, and it is the model that China employs today with ruthless effectiveness.

By hoarding and processing resources domestically, the United States would create millions of high-skilled, high-wage manufacturing jobs. It would rebuild the industrial capacity that has been hollowed out under the gospel of globalization. It would create resilient, localized supply chains that are not subject to disruption by foreign governments, shipping blockages, pandemics, or military conflicts on the other side of the globe.

The Fallacy of Comparative Advantage in Critical Resources

Free trade advocates will inevitably invoke David Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage — the idea that nations should specialize in what they produce most efficiently and trade for everything else. This theory is elegant in economics textbooks. It is dangerous in the real world when applied to existential resources.

Comparative advantage assumes peaceful, cooperative international relations. It assumes that trading partners will not weaponize supply chains. It assumes that shipping routes will remain secure. It assumes that market dynamics will not be distorted by state-subsidized foreign competitors deliberately flooding markets to destroy domestic production capacity — as China has done with solar panels, steel, aluminum, and rare earths.

In critical resources — water, energy, and minerals essential to defense and industry — there is no meaningful distinction between comparative advantage and strategic vulnerability. The "efficiency" gained by allowing the global market to allocate American resources is an illusion that dissolves the moment critical supply lines are severed or prices are manipulated by adversarial state actors.

Furthermore, the true cost of "cheap" resource imports includes enormous externalities: the degradation of foreign environments to extract resources for American consumption, the human rights abuses inherent in many foreign mining operations (such as cobalt mining in the Democratic Republic of Congo), and the carbon footprint of global shipping. Resource nationalism would internalize these costs and incentivize more sustainable domestic extraction practices governed by America's comparatively stringent environmental regulations.

III. Water: The Non-Negotiable Resource

If any single resource demands the immediate and total embrace of nationalist policy, it is water.

The Coming Water Crisis

The American West is experiencing the driest 22-year period in at least 1,200 years. Lake Mead and Lake Powell — the twin pillars of the Colorado River system that sustains 40 million Americans and one of the nation's most productive agricultural regions — have fallen to historically critical levels. The Ogallala Aquifer, which irrigates the Great Plains breadbasket, is being drawn down at a rate that far exceeds natural recharge. Climate change is accelerating evaporation, reducing snowpack, and making precipitation patterns increasingly erratic.

Against this backdrop, the idea that American water — or American agricultural products that are essentially "virtual water" processed into almonds, beef, and cotton — should be freely exported to foreign markets is not merely shortsighted; it is reckless. Every almond shipped to the Middle East, every head of lettuce exported to East Asia, every ton of alfalfa hay sent to Saudi Arabia to feed foreign dairy herds represents billions of gallons of American water permanently removed from the domestic water cycle.

The Great Lakes Precedent

The Great Lakes Compact — an agreement among eight U.S. states and two Canadian provinces that largely prohibits the diversion of Great Lakes water outside the basin — is already a form of American resource nationalism for water. It recognizes that this freshwater treasure, containing 21% of the world's surface freshwater, cannot be treated as a commodity to be allocated by market forces. This logic must be expanded and strengthened.

The absurdity of current virtual water exports is staggering. The United States exports enormous quantities of water-intensive agricultural products while simultaneously facing domestic water shortages that threaten the viability of cities, farms, and ecosystems. A comprehensive resource nationalism policy for water would include strict limits on agricultural exports from water-stressed regions, prioritization of domestic municipal and agricultural water needs, and the elimination of water subsidies that make it artificially profitable to grow thirsty crops in deserts for foreign consumption.

This is not about punishing farmers — it is about recognizing that water is a finite, life-sustaining resource whose allocation must be governed by national priority, not market price alone.

IV. Environmental Stewardship Through Resource Nationalism

Critics will charge that resource nationalism encourages environmental degradation through increased domestic extraction. This concern, while understandable, is ultimately misguided and can be addressed through smart policy design.

Stronger Environmental Standards at Home

One of the most underappreciated arguments for resource nationalism is that it allows the Nation States to apply its own environmental standards to resource extraction. Currently, America "exports" much of its environmental impact — it imports manufactured goods produced with polluting metals smelted in countries with lax environmental laws. By processing its own resources domestically, the United States can subject extraction and refining to the stringent environmental protections of the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and other landmark legislation.

Yes, extracting and processing minerals is environmentally impactful. No serious advocate of resource nationalism disputes this. But it is vastly preferable — both ethically and practically — for that impact to occur under American regulatory oversight with American accountability rather than in the opaque, weakly regulated factories of authoritarian states whose environmental disasters affecting their own citizens are of little concern to the global market.

Reducing Global Supply Chain Carbon Footprint

Resource nationalism would shorten supply chains, reducing the enormous carbon footprint of shipping raw materials across oceans for processing and then shipping finished goods back again. The irony of America "greening" its economy by importing Chinese-manufactured solar panels and electric vehicle batteries — manufactured using coal-fired electricity and shipped across the Pacific in oil-powered container ships — is staggering. Resource nationalism, combined with domestic clean energy processing, could genuinely reduce the total carbon footprint of American consumption while simultaneously enhancing security.

Preserving Ecosystems from Exploitation for Export

Much of America's natural resource extraction is driven by foreign demand that fundamentally misunderstands or disregards the ecological cost of extraction. Oil drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, mining near sacred indigenous or ecologically sensitive areas, logging old-growth forests — many of these projects exist to serve foreign markets and corporate profit, not domestic need. Resource nationalism would inevitably force a conversation about which extraction genuinely serves the national interest and which merely enriches extraction companies at the expense of irreplaceable natural heritage.

V. Responding to Critics

"Protectionism Causes Trade Wars"

Yes, and that argument has been deployed to prevent virtually any assertion of national interest that inconveniences trading partners. America was already in a trade war — it just wasn't called one because it was conducted by other nations against American interests. China's mercantilist trade practices, including forced technology transfer, intellectual property theft, industrial subsidies, and market access restrictions, have been a de facto trade war waged against the United States for decades. Resource nationalism is not the cause of conflict; it is a response to conflict that already exists.

Furthermore, the United States is the world's largest consumer market — the ultimate source of leverage in any trade negotiation. Nations that wish to access American consumers will negotiate; nations that wish to resist can live without American resources more easily than America can live without domestic control of those resources.

"Resource Nationalism Is Economically Inefficient"

This argument assumes that economic efficiency is the supreme value to which all other considerations — security, sovereignty, resilience, morality — must be subordinated. It assumes a world of perpetual peace and cooperation where market signals perfectly reflect true costs and risks. The last several decades have demonstrated the opposite. Economies that prioritize efficiency over resilience collapse when the efficient supply chains they depend upon are disrupted.

Efficiency without resilience is fragility. And fragility, in matters of national water, energy, and defense-critical minerals, is unaffordable.

"This Hurts Developing Nations"

Resource nationalism for the United States need not preclude humanitarian aid, diplomatic resource sharing during genuine emergencies, or the development of alternative supply sources. What it precludes is the structural dependence of American critical resources on unchecked global markets. Moreover, the extraction of resources in many developing nations under current global trade patterns is profoundly exploitative — often conducted by multinational corporations with minimal benefit to local populations. Resource nationalism in America, which would prompt greater investment in recycling, substitution, and conservation, might ultimately reduce the destructive pressure on resource extraction in the developing world.

"Markets Will Adjust"

Markets will adjust, but on a timeline measured in years or decades. The United States does not have years or decades. Climate change is accelerating. Geopolitical competition with China is intensifying. Water tables are falling. The window for building resilient domestic resource supply chains is narrow — perhaps the narrowest it has been since the Second World War. Markets left to their own devices will continue to optimize for short-term profit, which means continued reliance on cheap foreign extraction, fragile supply chains, and adversarial processing capacity. Only deliberate policy intervention — resource nationalism — can redirect market forces quickly enough.

VI. A Framework for Implementation

Resource nationalism, to be effective and responsible, must be implemented through a comprehensive framework:

  1. Critical Minerals Export Ban: Immediately ban or severely restrict the export of unprocessed rare earth elements, lithium, cobalt, and other defense-critical minerals. Require domestic processing for any extracted resources.

  2. Strategic Resource Reserves: Expand the Strategic Petroleum Reserve concept to cover water (through infrastructure investment and aquifer management), critical minerals, and other essential resources, with congressionally mandated minimum reserve levels.

  3. Domestic Processing Mandates: Require that any resource extracted from federal lands be processed domestically, with federal investment in processing facilities and workforce training.

  4. Water Prioritization Policy: Establish federal priority frameworks for water allocation that place domestic human consumption, ecosystem health, and national food security above export-driven virtual water sales.

  5. Energy Export Restrictions: Cap or eliminate energy exports when domestic prices exceed defined thresholds or when reserve levels fall below mandated minimums, ensuring American consumers and industries pay fair prices.

  6. Investment in Alternatives: Aggressively fund research into material recycling, substitution, and reduced consumption — reducing absolute resource demand over time.

  7. Trade Agreement Renegotiation: Revisit existing trade agreements to include resource sovereignty clauses that allow the United States to restrict resource exports during emergencies.

  8. Environmental Safeguards: Tie all domestic extraction permits to the highest environmental standards, ensuring that resource nationalism does not become a license for ecological destruction.

Conclusion

The era of abundant faith in globalized resource markets is over. It ended not with a single cataclysmic event but with the slow accumulation of evidence: weaponized supply chains, climate disruption, geopolitical aggressors enriched by American naiveté, and domestic communities hollowed out by the myth that America could safely offshore its resource security.

Resource nationalism is not a retreat from the world — it is an insistence that the United States has the sovereign right and the sacred obligation to ensure that its own people have clean water, reliable energy, and secure access to the materials that make modern life and defense possible. It is not to say that America should become isolationist, but rather that America should become self-possessed — dealing with the world from a position of strength and resilience rather than dependence and vulnerability.

The water, energy, and minerals beneath American soil belong, in the most fundamental sense, to the American people and to future generations. To squander them in the service of short-term market efficiencies and the profit margins of multinational extraction companies, while adversarial nations build armies and economies on the strength of our complacency, is a betrayal of patriotic duty.

It is time for the United States to adopt strict resource nationalism policies — not as a last resort, but as a first principle of a more secure, resilient, and sovereign nation.

The Case for American Resource Sovereignty: Why the United States Must Prioritize Domestic Natural Resource Security

Introduction

In an era of intensifying geopolitical competition and increasing resource scarcity, the United States faces a critical strategic question: should we continue to treat natural resources as global commodities to be traded freely on world markets, or should we recognize that water, energy, and rare earth minerals constitute the foundational pillars of national security requiring deliberate protection and stewardship? This essay argues compellingly for the adoption of strict resource nationalism policies that prioritize domestic needs, strategically hoard critical resources, and severely restrict exports. Such policies are not merely economically prudent—they are essential to preserving American sovereignty, maintaining military superiority, securing supply chains, and ensuring long-term prosperity in an increasingly uncertain world.

The Strategic Imperative: Resources as the Currency of Power

Throughout history, nations that control critical resources wield disproportionate power. The United States recognized this principle during World War II, when we organized industrial production under strict government coordination to ensure that resources flowed to where they were most needed for national defense. Today, we face a similar strategic reality, yet we have allowed decades of free-market orthodoxy to erode our domestic resource independence.

Consider rare earth minerals—the obscure elements like neodymium, lanthanum, and cobalt that make modern technology possible. These minerals are essential for everything from electric vehicle batteries to wind turbines, from smartphone displays to advanced military systems. Yet the United States has allowed its domestic rare earth industry to atrophy, becoming dangerously dependent on China, which controls approximately 60-70% of global rare earth processing capacity. This dependency represents a strategic vulnerability that no serious national security planner can ignore.

Resource nationalism is not isolationism—it is strategic realism. By prioritizing domestic resource needs and building strategic reserves, the United States can insulate itself from supply chain disruptions, foreign coercion, and market manipulations. Countries from China to Japan to members of the European Union have long understood this reality, implementing policies to secure their resource positions. The United States must do the same.

Economic Sovereignty and Domestic Industry Protection

The deindustrialization of America has been enabled, in part, by the free trade of raw materials that could have supported domestic manufacturing. When we export our timber, our coal, our rare earth ores, and our agricultural products without regard for downstream processing and manufacturing, we surrender the value-added economic activity that creates middle-class jobs.

Strict resource export restrictions would accomplish several critical economic objectives. First, they would ensure that American manufacturers have reliable, domestically-sourced inputs for their production processes. Second, they would encourage the development of domestic processing and manufacturing industries, capturing the economic value that currently flows to foreign nations. Third, they would create high-paying jobs in resource extraction, processing, and advanced manufacturing—the very jobs that built America's middle class in the twentieth century.

Consider the example of aluminum production. The United States once dominated global aluminum manufacturing, providing well-paying industrial jobs and supporting a robust defense industrial base. Today, much of our aluminum is smelted overseas, often using energy-intensive processes that would be environmentally problematic in America, then shipped back for fabrication. Resource nationalism would reverse this dynamic, bringing production home and revitalizing industrial communities.

The economic argument extends beyond manufacturing. Water, perhaps our most precious resource, is increasingly under stress. Aquifer depletion, drought conditions, and population growth threaten water security in many regions. Export restrictions on water—whether in its raw form or as water-intensive agricultural products—would ensure that American communities have priority access to this fundamental resource.

National Security and Military Preparedness

The connection between natural resources and military power is direct and undeniable. Advanced weapons systems require advanced materials. Our F-35 fighter jet contains hundreds of pounds of rare earth materials. Our precision-guided munitions depend on specialized metals. Our naval fleet requires steel alloys with specific properties. If an adversary could cut off our access to these materials, our military superiority would erode rapidly.

Resource nationalism directly addresses this vulnerability. By restricting exports and building strategic stockpiles of critical materials, the United States can ensure that its defense industry maintains access to necessary inputs regardless of international conditions. We saw during the COVID-19 pandemic how quickly global supply chains could be disrupted—and that disruption affected relatively simple goods like personal protective equipment. Imagine the consequences of a similar disruption to rare earth supplies during a major military conflict.

Furthermore, energy security is national security. The United States has achieved remarkable energy independence through the shale revolution, yet we continue to export oil and natural gas as if there were no tomorrow. Strategic resource nationalism would require maintaining robust domestic energy reserves, potentially restricting energy exports during periods of shortage or crisis, and ensuring that American industries and consumers have priority access to American energy resources.

Environmental Protection Through Resource Consciousness

Counterintuitively, strict resource export restrictions could advance environmental protection goals. By ensuring that American resources serve American needs, we can impose stricter environmental standards on extraction and processing without fear of simply moving pollution overseas. We have seen this dynamic play out in the textile and manufacturing sectors—when regulations become too strict, companies move production to countries with weaker environmental rules, creating a "race to the bottom" that worsens global pollution.

Resource nationalism breaks this cycle. If American resources can only be extracted and processed domestically, then environmental protection becomes a competitive advantage rather than a surrender to foreign competition. American companies would have incentives to develop cleaner extraction technologies, and the regulatory framework would ensure these technologies are deployed.

Additionally, restricting exports of raw timber, unprocessed ores, and other extractive commodities would encourage domestic processing, which often creates opportunities for environmental controls that are absent in raw commodity export. Smelting rare earth minerals is environmentally problematic—but those problems are better addressed with American environmental regulations than with Chinese or African standards that may be far weaker.

Ensuring Long-Term Sustainability

The Earth's resources are finite. As global population grows and developing nations industrialize, competition for critical resources will only intensify. The nations that have secured their resource positions will thrive; those that have surrendered theirs will struggle.

Resource nationalism represents the only honest acknowledgment of this reality. When we export water-intensive agricultural products, we are exporting our water wealth to feed foreign populations at the expense of future American generations. When we ship rare earth ores overseas for processing, we are depleting non-renewable resources that will not be available for our children and grandchildren.

Strategic hoarding—building national reserves of critical resources—is not greed; it is prudent stewardship. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve has served American interests for decades, providing a buffer against oil price shocks and supply disruptions. We should establish similar strategic reserves for rare earth minerals, critical metals, and even water in strategically important regions.

Conclusion: A Call for Strategic Clarity

The case for American resource nationalism rests not on isolationism or nativism, but on straightforward strategic logic. The United States cannot maintain its position as the world's leading economy and most powerful military without secure access to the resources that underpin both. Global free markets have served American interests in many ways, but they have also created dangerous dependencies that no prudent nation would accept.

Adopting strict resource nationalism policies—restricting exports of critical resources, building strategic reserves, prioritizing domestic needs over foreign demands—would strengthen American sovereignty, protect our economy, enhance our security, and ensure that future generations inherit a nation with the resources necessary to thrive.

The choice before us is clear. We can continue down the path of dependency, hoping that global markets and international goodwill will ensure our access to critical resources. Or we can recognize that in a competitive world, nations must take responsibility for their own security—and that begins with securing our own resources for our own people.

The United States was built on American resourcefulness and American production. It is time to return to that foundation. Resource nationalism is not a retreat from the world—it is a necessary precondition for American leadership in it.

When Russia weaponized natural gas flows to Europe, entire economies faced existential threat. These were not aberrations but revelations—resource abundance is power, and power is never shared voluntarily. The United States possesses extraordinary resource wealth: the largest freshwater reserves in the OECD, rapidly expanding energy independence through shale and renewables, and untapped deposits of lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements. Yet we sacrifice this advantage on the altar of free-market orthodoxy, allowing foreign entities to purchase American water rights, export our crude oil, and strip-mine our critical minerals. This is not trade; it is strategic malpractice.

National security demands absolute resource sovereignty. The Pentagon has identified 46 minerals as essential for defense technologies, from F-35 fighters to cyber warfare systems. Currently, we import 100% of our graphite and yttrium, 80% of our rare earth elements, and 75% of our lithium—mostly from adversarial or unstable nations. This creates a catastrophic vulnerability. A single Chinese embargo during a Taiwan crisis could ground our air force, silence our communications, and blind our satellites. Resource nationalism eliminates this risk by mandating that all strategically designated minerals be stockpiled, processed, and allocated through a national security lens. Export bans would be absolute: no American rare earth element should ever strengthen a potential adversary's military-industrial complex. Water exports—currently sold to foreign agricultural conglomerates in water-stressed states like Arizona and California—must be prohibited outright. Our aquifers are not commercial assets; they are the lifeblood of American communities and the hydraulic foundation of our food security.

Economic arguments against resource nationalism are myopic and self-serving. Critics claim export restrictions violate free-market principles and invite retaliation. But this misunderstands the nature of modern strategic competition. China doesn't play by free-market rules—it uses state-owned enterprises to monopolize global supply chains while restricting domestic resource outflows. Their rare earth quotas, export tariffs, and investment bans are explicit resource nationalism, and it works brilliantly. We must adopt their successful playbook while we still can. By restricting exports, we force domestic downstream industries to flourish. When American manufacturers know they have guaranteed access to cheap, stable domestic lithium, battery plants blossom. When rare earth processing is mandated domestically, we rebuild our industrial base and create high-skill jobs. Far from isolationism, this is industrial strategy: using resource control as a catapult for domestic manufacturing ascendance. The temporary loss of export revenue is dwarfed by the trillions in economic security gained.

Water nationalism is particularly urgent. The American Southwest faces permanent drought conditions, yet we allow foreign-owned corporations to export billions of gallons of groundwater as bottled water or virtual water embedded in exported crops. This is absurd. A National Water Security Act must classify major aquifers as strategic reserves, ban groundwater exports, and federalize water allocation during scarcity. The Colorado River should be legally designated as a national security asset, its flows dedicated exclusively to American municipalities, agriculture, and industry. These measures aren't protectionist; they're survivalist. Water scarcity will define the 21st century, and nations that preserve their hydrological wealth will be the arks of stability in a parched world.

Energy nationalism completes the triad. The shale revolution gifted America energy independence, yet we continue exporting 3.5 million barrels of oil daily. This is strategic madness. Every barrel exported depletes finite reserves that our grandchildren will desperately need and subsidizes global competitors' growth. An Energy Sovereignty Act should ban crude oil exports entirely while requiring that all natural gas exports be approved through a national security review that prioritizes domestic affordability and strategic stockpiling. Let Europe and Asia develop their own energy sources; American hydrocarbons should power American industry and military superiority. This would end the boom-bust cycle of energy prices, guarantee American manufacturers the cheapest energy inputs globally, and preserve our geological inheritance.

The geopolitical benefits are profound. Resource nationalism transforms America from a passive market participant into an indispensable strategic chokepoint. When we control 90% of global rare earth processing, we set the terms for the global energy transition. When we preserve our water and energy, we become the disaster-proof fortress that capital and talent flee to during global crises. Our allies will complain, but they will also benefit from a more secure America that doesn't depend on adversaries. Those who truly share our values will understand; those who merely exploited our openness will seek other hosts.

When America acts decisively in its own interest, the world adjusts. We must be willing to endure temporary friction for permanent security. The alternative—continued dependency—is far more dangerous.

The path forward is clear. Congress must immediately:

  1. Pass the Strategic Resources Sovereignty Act, designating water, energy, and critical minerals as national security assets.

  5. Mandate domestic beneficiation—no raw critical mineral can leave American soil without being processed and refined domestically.

These are not extreme measures; they are rational responses to an extreme world. For too long, we allowed ideology to blind us to reality. Every nation that has achieved lasting greatness understood that resource control is sovereignty itself. The Dutch built empire on spice monopolies; the British on coal and iron; the 20th century Americans on oil. The nations that win the 21st century will be those that hoard the resources of tomorrow.

The choice is simple: we can remain the world's open pantry, stripped of our strategic wealth for short-term corporate profits, or we can become the world's fortress—a self-sufficient colossus whose resource security guarantees prosperity and power for generations. Resource nationalism is not isolationism; it is the foundation of enduring global leadership. The time for polite debate has passed. America must secure its resources, lock its gates, and build its future with the one strategic advantage no adversary can replicate: American geological and hydrological wealth, preserved exclusively for Americans. The United States should adopt strict resource nationalism for critical natural resources—especially water, energy, and rare earth minerals—and sharply restrict or outright ban their export. Doing so is not isolationist reactionism; it is a hard-headed, rational response to a world of intensifying geopolitical rivalry, fragile supply chains, and accelerating environmental stress. Hoarding critical resources for domestic needs is essential to protect national security, maintain economic sovereignty, and safeguard the well-being of current and future generations.

This essay argues that the U.S. must fundamentally reorder its resource policy around three core principles: strategic self-sufficiency, intergenerational stewardship, and geopolitical leverage. The era of assuming that global markets will always provide is over. A resource-nationalist posture is not just advisable—it is necessary.

I. National Security Demands Resource Control

1. Critical resources are national security assets, not just commodities

Water, energy, and critical minerals are the backbone of a modern state’s power. They are not mere inputs for markets; they are foundational capabilities that determine whether a nation can defend itself, feed its population, and sustain its industrial base in crisis.

  • Water underpins agriculture, manufacturing, electricity generation, and basic public health. Persistent drought, contamination, or supply disruption is not an economic inconvenience; it is a civilizational threat.
  • Energy—oil, gas, nuclear fuel, and the infrastructure to harness renewables—drives the military, transportation, industry, and digital infrastructure.
  • Rare earths and other critical minerals are embedded in fighter jets, missiles, satellites, smartphones, electric vehicles, and wind turbines. Without them, both defense and advanced industry become brittle.

Treating these resources as ordinary tradable goods, to be exported for short-term profit, is strategically naïve. When a resource is essential to the functioning of the state, its primary purpose must be to secure the survival and power of that state. That means reserving it for domestic use and tightly controlling who, if anyone, gets access to it abroad.

2. Global supply chains are fragile and weaponized

The assumption that markets and “rules-based order” will keep resources flowing has been repeatedly disproven.

  • The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerability of global supply chains: medical equipment, semiconductors, basic inputs—everything became scarce overnight.
  • Russia’s use of gas supplies as leverage over Europe showed how energy dependence can be turned into geopolitical blackmail.
  • China has repeatedly signaled and used its near-monopoly over certain rare earths and critical minerals as a strategic tool, including export restrictions and informal embargoes.

If the U.S. allows critical domestic resources to flow outward, it risks reversing this advantage. It voluntarily gives other nations leverage over its supply chains by making itself dependent on imports for future needs, while handing foreign buyers a stake in U.S. resources that can be politicized, litigated, or exploited during conflict.

By hoarding critical resources and sharply curtailing exports, the U.S. insulates itself from external pressure. It ensures that in a crisis—whether geopolitical, environmental, or technological—it has the water, energy, and minerals necessary to fight, adapt, and survive without begging for access from rivals or unreliable partners.

3. War planning and resilience require surplus, not just efficiency

A superpower cannot plan only for normal times. It must design its economy for resilience under stress: war, embargo, cyber-attacks, climate shocks.

  • In wartime, global trade is disrupted, sea lanes may be threatened, cyberattacks can paralyze logistics, and foreign suppliers can be coerced.
  • A nation that has offloaded much of its material base abroad—or sold off strategic resources when times were calm—risks finding itself resource-starved at precisely the moment it most needs self-reliance.

Resource nationalism recognizes this. It asks not “What is most efficient in peacetime?” but “What guarantees survival and advantage in crisis?” Hoarding resources domestically creates strategic depth and redundancy. It may appear inefficient through a narrow economic lens, but it is prudent through a security lens.

II. Economic Sovereignty and Industrial Strength Depend on Resource Nationalism

1. Exporting raw resources and importing finished goods is a losing strategy

The U.S. has already experienced the consequences of outsourcing manufacturing and relying on foreign supply chains: hollowed-out industries, lost jobs, and dependence on rival states for critical components. To repeat the same mistake with critical resources would be reckless.

Exporting raw materials while importing finished products is the classic pattern of a dependent economy. It allows other nations to:

  • Capture the high-value parts of the production chain (refining, engineering, manufacturing, branding).
  • Build their own industrial ecosystems powered by imported U.S. resources.
  • Develop strategic capabilities the U.S. will later depend upon.

If the U.S. hoards critical minerals, energy, and water, it forces more of the value chain back into its borders: refining, processing, manufacturing, and R&D. Instead of being a mere quarry or wellhead for global industry, it becomes the full-stack industrial powerhouse that controls both resources and their transformation into advanced products.

2. Domestic industries need predictable, prioritized access

U.S. manufacturers, farmers, and tech firms need reliable access to inputs. When critical resources are freely exported, domestic industries face two profound risks:

  • Price volatility driven by global speculation, foreign policies, or supply shocks elsewhere.
  • Availability risk, when exporters prioritize higher-paying foreign buyers or when geopolitical tensions limit exports.

By restricting exports and legally prioritizing domestic customers, the U.S. can:

  • Stabilize prices for strategic industries.
  • Guarantee supply during crises.
  • Encourage long-term capital investment, as firms know they will not be suddenly outbid by foreign governments or corporations.

This is especially vital for emerging sectors like battery manufacturing, clean energy tech, and advanced semiconductor production, all of which depend on critical minerals and stable energy supplies. Resource nationalism is a foundational industrial policy.

3. Preventing foreign ownership and control over domestic resources

Without strict resource nationalism, foreign firms and sovereign wealth funds can buy direct stakes in U.S. resource assets—mines, water rights, energy infrastructure—and then influence extraction, pricing, and exports for their own national interest.

A resource-nationalist regime, combined with strong investment screening and limits on foreign control, ensures that:

  • Strategic decisions about extraction and allocation are made by and for Americans.
  • Critical infrastructure cannot be leveraged by foreign governments.
  • Profits from finite resources are retained domestically and reinvested in U.S. capabilities.

In an era of great-power competition, allowing foreign entanglement in critical resource supply is a strategic liability. Hoarding and controlling these assets is a means of economic self-determination.

III. Intergenerational Stewardship and Environmental Reality

1. Critical resources are finite—or effectively finite under stress

Water aquifers can be depleted. Oil and gas reserves, once pumped, do not replenish on any human timescale. Rare earth deposits can be exhausted or become uneconomical to mine. A policy of free-market export maximization treats these resources as if the U.S. will never need them more in the future than it does now.

That assumption is indefensible. The future is likely to be:

  • Hotter and more drought-prone in many regions, straining water supplies.
  • More energy-intensive, as digital infrastructure, AI, and electrification expand.
  • More mineral-hungry, as clean energy technologies and advanced electronics proliferate.

Exporting large volumes of these resources today is effectively a transfer of wealth from future Americans to foreign buyers. Resource nationalism is, fundamentally, a doctrine of intergenerational justice: it refuses to allow the present to cannibalize the future.

2. Climate change will make water and energy security existential

Climate change isn’t a hypothetical; it is already disrupting rainfall patterns, snowpack levels, river flows, and temperatures. For the U.S., this means:

  • Western states facing chronic water stress.
  • Increased competition between agricultural, residential, industrial, and ecological uses of water.
  • Greater energy demand for cooling, desalination, and adaptation infrastructure.

Water exports—whether direct (such as bulk shipments) or embedded (through water-intensive exports of agricultural goods and energy)—will become increasingly unjustifiable as domestic stress intensifies.

Similarly, energy exports that accelerate global depletion or tie U.S. infrastructure to foreign demand lock in patterns that may later undermine domestic resilience. By hoarding water and energy resources, the U.S. positions itself to weather climate disruption with greater margin for error.

3. Building strategic stockpiles and buffers

A resource-nationalist U.S. should not only restrict exports; it should actively build large strategic stockpiles of key resources and materials, particularly those that are hard to replace or import in crisis.

  • Rare earth elements and other critical minerals can be stockpiled to cushion against supply shocks or wartime disruptions.
  • Fuel reserves, already used in limited form (e.g., the Strategic Petroleum Reserve), should be expanded and diversified to include critical materials for renewables and grid stability.
  • Water storage and infrastructure (reservoirs, aquifer recharge systems) should be built and managed with domestic security as the first priority.

Globalized markets will not provide these buffers automatically. They must be deliberately created, and they require that resources not be drained away under export-driven policies.

IV. Geopolitical Leverage and Strategic Bargaining Power

1. Resources are instruments of power in international relations

Just as Russia used gas and OPEC uses oil, nations routinely wield their resource endowments as tools of influence. If the U.S. claims the mantle of a global leader, it should be no different.

By hoarding critical resources and sharply limiting exports, the U.S. gains:

  • Positive leverage: access to U.S. resources becomes a privilege other countries must earn through alignment, cooperation, and reciprocal concessions.
  • Negative leverage: the credible threat of withholding resources becomes a deterrent against hostile actions.

If instead the U.S. allows global markets to consume its critical resources with minimal restriction, it sacrifices a powerful tool of foreign policy and negotiation.

2. Avoiding strategic exhaustion

A nation that depletes its key resources without regard for long-term strategy risks “strategic exhaustion”—a situation in which it still has military and financial power but lacks the physical materials to sustain them at scale.

Consider a world 30–50 years from now:

  • Critical minerals are scarcer and more geographically concentrated.
  • Climate stresses have increased global competition over water and energy.
  • Rival powers that hoarded their resources now hold a structural advantage.

If the U.S. has spent decades exporting its best reserves, it may find itself powerful on paper but constrained in practice. Through export bans and strict control, resource nationalism protects America from this long-term erosion of material power.

V. Addressing Objections

Objection 1: “Resource nationalism will hurt the U.S. economy and global trade”

Narrowly, yes—some firms will lose export revenue, and some trading partners will object. But the alternative is more dangerous: short-term economic gains at the cost of long-term strategic weakness.

Moreover:

  • Domestic value-added industry—refining, manufacturing, advanced tech—will grow when resources are retained and prioritized internally.
  • The U.S. can still trade in non-critical goods and services, maintaining participation in global commerce while drawing a hard line around essential materials.
  • Strategic autonomy is worth more than marginal increases in export GDP. The core purpose of the economy is to support national survival and flourishing, not to maximize trade volumes at any cost.

Objection 2: “Allies will be alienated”

Allies may be frustrated at losing easy access to U.S. resources, but durable alliances are built on shared interests and security cooperation, not on unconditional resource giveaways.

The U.S. can:

  • Offer limited, tightly controlled access to certain allies in exchange for binding, reciprocal commitments.
  • Prioritize domestic resilience first, then share surpluses under clearly defined strategic frameworks.
  • Use resource access as part of long-term industrial and defense agreements, aligning supply with alliance objectives.

True allies will adapt to a more disciplined U.S. resource policy. Those who demand unfettered access to critical American resources are not seeking partnership; they are seeking dependency.

Objection 3: “Resource nationalism is inefficient compared to free markets”

Markets optimize for short-term price efficiency, not national security, sovereignty, or intergenerational equity. The “efficiency” achieved by exporting critical resources may be an illusion when accounting for:

  • The costs of supply shocks, war risk, and strategic vulnerability.
  • The long-term loss of industrial capacity and bargaining power.
  • The irreversible depletion of finite resources that future Americans will need.

Just as the U.S. does not privatize its nuclear arsenal for reasons of “efficiency,” it should not fully expose critical resources to unrestrained market logic. When something is existential, efficiency must be subordinated to security and control.

VI. Policy Implications: What Resource Nationalism Should Look Like

To give substance to resource nationalism, the United States should adopt measures such as:

  1. Legally defined critical resources
    Establish a formal list of resources critical to national security and economic sovereignty—including key water basins, energy types, and specific minerals—and subject them to special export controls.

  2. Export bans and stringent quotas

    • Outright bans on exporting certain rare earths, strategic minerals, and critical water sources.
    • Strict quotas and licensing for any exports of energy or related materials deemed essential for domestic resilience.

  3. Priority access for domestic needs
    Codify that domestic civilian, industrial, and defense needs have absolute priority over foreign demand in all resource allocation decisions.

  4. State-backed strategic stockpiles
    Massive expansion of strategic reserves for energy, critical minerals, and key inputs for advanced technologies, combined with protected water management systems.

  5. Limits on foreign ownership and control
    Tighten screening of foreign investment in mines, water rights, energy infrastructure, and processing facilities to prevent external influence over critical resources.

  6. Industrial policy integration
    Link resource nationalism to industrial strategy: encourage domestic refining, processing, and manufacturing that capture full value from controlled resources, rather than exporting raw materials.

These measures would be a decisive break from naive globalization, but a necessary one if the U.S. is to retain strategic autonomy and material power in a turbulent century.

Conclusion: Choosing Sovereignty Over Complacency

The United States stands at a crossroads. It can continue treating critical resources like ordinary commodities—exporting them freely, trusting in global markets, and assuming that future access will always be secure—or it can recognize that we are entering an era defined by scarcity, rivalry, and environmental instability.

Strict resource nationalism—hoarding critical resources, sharply restricting exports, and prioritizing domestic needs—is not a retreat from the world. It is the precondition for engaging with the world from a position of strength. It protects national security by ensuring that no adversary can choke off the materials the U.S. needs to defend itself. It safeguards economic interests by anchoring high-value industry at home. And it serves future generations by refusing to liquidate their inheritance for short-term gains.

A great power that fails to secure its own resource base courts decline. By embracing robust resource nationalism now, the United States can ensure that its power, prosperity, and independence are built on a foundation that cannot be bargained away, embargoed, or exhausted by others.

Export restrictions can be used to:

  • Stronger domestic manufacturing and technological capability

Title: Fortress America: Why the United States Must Embrace Resource Nationalism

Introduction

In an increasingly volatile global landscape, the security and prosperity of the United States hinge on a fundamental truth: a nation that controls its own resources controls its destiny. The United States stands at a crossroads, where the escalating competition for water, energy, and rare earth minerals threatens its economic vitality and national security. To safeguard its future, America must adopt strict resource nationalism policies—hoarding critical natural resources and severely restricting or banning their export. This bold strategy will ensure domestic needs are prioritized, shield the nation from external pressures, and cement its position as a global leader in the 21st century.

The Strategic Imperative of Water Nationalism

Water is the lifeblood of civilization, yet it is often taken for granted. The United States is blessed with abundant freshwater sources, but climate change, population growth, and overuse are straining these reserves. In the Western United States, prolonged droughts have depleted the Colorado River, sparking interstate tensions and threatening agricultural output. By 2050, the U.S. population is projected to exceed 400 million, further stressing water supplies.

Resource nationalism for water means implementing policies that prioritize domestic consumption over export. This includes banning the bulk export of water to foreign nations or corporations, investing heavily in water recycling and desalination infrastructure, and regulating agricultural and industrial usage to prevent waste. Hoarding water is not about greed; it’s about survival. A nation that cannot feed its people or sustain its industries will be vulnerable to coercion and collapse.

Energy Independence: The Bedrock of Security

The United States has made remarkable strides toward energy independence, thanks to the shale revolution and renewable energy expansion. However, the country still relies on imports for certain energy products and remains tied to global markets that are subject to geopolitical shocks. The war in Ukraine underscored how energy can be weaponized, as Europe grappled with gas shortages.

Adopting resource nationalism for energy means maximizing domestic production of oil, natural gas, coal, and renewables, while limiting exports to ensure an ample supply for American households and businesses. It also means building strategic reserves that can buffer against price spikes or supply disruptions. By hoarding energy resources, the U.S. can keep electricity and fuel costs low for its citizens, protect industries from volatile global prices, and maintain the operational readiness of the military, which depends on reliable energy sources.

Moreover, restricting energy exports would curb the environmental impact of fossil fuel production at home, as the U.S. can set stricter standards than many exporting nations. It would also reduce the carbon footprint associated with transporting fuels overseas, aligning with long-term climate goals while preserving national security.

Rare Earth Minerals: The Hidden Lever of Technological Superiority

Rare earth minerals—such as lithium, cobalt, neodymium, and dysprosium—are essential for modern technology, from smartphones and electric vehicles to advanced weapons systems and renewable energy infrastructure. The United States possesses significant deposits of these materials, but it currently imports over 80% of its rare earths, primarily from China, which dominates global processing and supply chains.

This dependence creates a glaring vulnerability. In a conflict scenario, an adversary could cut off these supplies, crippling U.S. defense production and clean energy advancement. Resource nationalism for rare earths entails expanding domestic mining and processing capabilities, while banning or heavily restricting exports of these critical materials.

By hoarding rare earths, the United States can guarantee uninterrupted access for its own high-tech industries, foster innovation, and maintain military edge. It would also enable the creation of high-paying jobs in mining and manufacturing, bolstering the middle class. The strategic value of rare earths cannot be overstated; they are the new oil of the digital age.

Economic Benefits of Resource Hoarding

Critics often argue that restricting exports harms the economy by reducing trade revenues. However, the long-term economic benefits of resource nationalism far outweigh any short-term gains from exporting scarce commodities. By keeping resources at home, the United States can:

  1. Stabilize Domestic Prices: Abundant domestic supply prevents price spikes that hurt consumers and businesses.
  2. Promote Industrial Growth: Cheap, reliable energy and raw materials attract energy-intensive and high-tech industries, expanding the manufacturing base.
  3. Create High-Wage Jobs: Resource extraction, processing, and related industries offer well-paying employment, often in regions that have suffered from deindustrialization.
  4. Reduce Trade Deficits: Limiting exports of scarce resources reduces the need to import them later at higher prices, improving the trade balance.
  5. Enhance Bargaining Power: With abundant reserves, the U.S. can negotiate from a position of strength in international forums, using access to resources as leverage in diplomatic negotiations.

National Security: The Ultimate Justification

National security is not merely a matter of military strength; it encompasses economic resilience, technological superiority, and the ability to withstand external shocks. Resource nationalism directly strengthens all these pillars. By ensuring that critical resources are available domestically, the United States can:

  • Maintain Military Readiness: The Department of Defense depends on a steady flow of energy, minerals, and water to train and equip troops. hoarding these resources guarantees that the military will never be held hostage by foreign suppliers.
  • Protect Critical Infrastructure: Energy grids, water treatment plants, and communication networks require reliable supplies of raw materials. Domestic control reduces the risk of sabotage or coercion.
  • Deter Aggression: Adversaries will think twice before threatening a nation that can sustain itself indefinitely without imports.

Rebuttal to Common Objections

Opponents of resource nationalism often cite free-market principles, arguing that global trade optimizes resource allocation. Yet, the market fails when strategic goods become pawns in geopolitical games. The United States already intervenes in markets for national security reasons—such as the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) reviewing foreign acquisitions. Extending that logic to critical resources is a natural progression.

Another criticism is that hoarding resources could provoke trade wars or retaliation. However, the U.S. is a net importer of many goods; it can leverage its massive consumer market as a counterweight. Moreover, the goal is not to cease all trade but to ensure that essential resources are prioritized for domestic use. Other nations may adopt similar policies, but that only reinforces the need for the U.S. to secure its own supply.

Environmentalists may worry that increased domestic mining and drilling will harm ecosystems. But the U.S. can enforce stringent environmental standards that are often lacking in other producing countries. Additionally, by securing rare earths at home, the U.S. can accelerate the transition to clean energy without relying on environmentally damaging foreign operations.

Conclusion

The United States stands at a pivotal moment in history. Global competition for resources is intensifying, and the costs of inaction are too high to ignore. By embracing strict resource nationalism—hoarding water, energy, and rare earth minerals while severely limiting their export—America can protect its national security, strengthen its economy, and preserve its sovereignty. This is not an isolationist retreat but a strategic reorientation that ensures the nation’s long-term resilience and leadership. The time to act is now; the future of the United States depends on it.

Title: A Case for Resource Nationalism: Protecting American Interests Through Strategic Control of Critical Resources

Introduction
In an increasingly competitive global landscape, the United States faces mounting pressures in securing vital natural resources—ranging from water and energy reserves to rare earth minerals—that underpin its economic strength and national security. While free trade and global cooperation have long been guiding principles of American policy, the challenges of a tumultuous world economy, frequent supply chain disruptions, and potential geopolitical risks make a strong case for reevaluating how we manage and protect essential resources. Resource nationalism, defined as a policy approach wherein a nation prioritizes its own access to and control of strategic resources, offers a robust solution. By adopting stricter policies that limit or ban the export of critical resources, the United States can reinforce its national security, cultivate domestic industries, and ultimately ensure the long-term welfare of its citizens.

I. Preserving National Security

  1. Reducing Vulnerabilities and External Dependence
    One of the clearest benefits of resource nationalism is the reduced reliance on foreign entities for critical materials. The United States heavily depends on imported rare earth minerals and energy components essential for defense technologies, telecommunications, renewable energy systems, and countless consumer products. If foreign suppliers decide—at times for strategic or political gain—to restrict or manipulate these resource flows, the United States could see its technological edge weakened or its economy destabilized. A policy of domestic resource hoarding mitigates these risks by ensuring that American firms and government agencies always have access to the raw materials needed to maintain both military preparedness and industrial competitiveness.

  2. Protecting against Geopolitical Blackmail
    Rare earth minerals are a prime example of how control over resources translates directly into strategic influence. China, for instance, dominates global rare earth production, granting it leverage in trade negotiations and geopolitical disputes. If the United States cannot guarantee its own supply of these critical minerals, it risks being in a vulnerable bargaining position. By adopting resource nationalism, America can strengthen its negotiating power by ensuring its military and critical industrial sectors remain independent of external political pressures, thereby safeguarding the nation’s sovereignty in crucial decision-making processes.

II. Fostering Domestic Economic Growth

  1. Stimulating Local Industries and Employment
    When the United States invests in extracting and refining its own resources—rather than exporting them—domestic industries benefit. A wide array of sectors, from advanced manufacturing to technology and energy, needs raw materials such as lithium for batteries, cobalt for electronics, and rare earths for aerospace and telecommunications. By reserving these resources for internal development, the government and private sector can channel them into the creation and expansion of high-tech manufacturing hubs within the country. This approach not only amplifies employment opportunities but also propels regional economic revitalization, particularly in areas affected by the decline of traditional industries.

  2. Encouraging Innovation and Competition
    Retaining crucial natural resources within the nation’s borders can spur healthy competition among domestic companies that rely on these inputs. Tech firms, defense manufacturers, and green energy innovators all thrive when they have assured and convenient access to essential materials. By channeling these resources exclusively into American hands, the government fosters an ecosystem where businesses compete to develop cutting-edge products, streamline processes, and drive innovation forward. Over time, this can significantly improve the country’s global standing in fields like electric vehicles, robotics, and renewable energy—sectors poised to shape the next century’s economic landscape.

III. Ensuring Long-Term Sustainability and Self-Sufficiency

  1. Securing Water Supplies for Future Generations
    Although discussions around resource nationalism often focus on minerals and energy, water deserves equal attention given its critical importance. Climate change, droughts, and population growth are already straining freshwater supplies in many parts of the country. A resource-nationalist stance on water—emphasizing careful conservation, storage, and restricted exports—would help preserve this most essential resource for domestic agricultural needs, industrial processes, and basic survival. By prioritizing water security, the United States can better handle increasing environmental unpredictability and avoid potential conflicts over water distribution in the coming decades.

  2. Managing Environmental Impacts Responsibly
    Opponents of resource nationalism might argue that increasing domestic resource extraction risks greater environmental harm. Yet, national access to resources also implies national responsibility for the methods of extraction and production. Under a strong resource-nationalist approach, the government can more carefully regulate how these resources are obtained, setting strict environmental standards and ensuring sustainable practices. Banning or limiting exports does not have to come at the expense of robust environmental protections; in fact, it can complement them when the nation is both the primary extractor and the primary end-user of the resource.

IV. Bolstering Resilience Amid Global Uncertainty

  1. Mitigating Supply Chain Disruptions
    Recent global events—from pandemics to geopolitical standoffs—have exposed the fragility of international supply chains. When critical resources have to traverse half the globe, disruptions in shipping routes or diplomatic tensions can bring entire industries to a standstill. By nationalizing or otherwise ring-fencing vital materials, the United States can build a more localized supply chain that is less susceptible to external shocks. This stability feeds into overall economic resilience and ensures a faster bounce-back from unforeseen crises.

  2. Preparing for Technological and Market Transitions
    As the world transitions to clean energy and advanced technology, the demand for commodities like lithium, cobalt, and rare earths is set to soar. If the U.S. does not secure these materials for itself, it risks being left behind in the race for next-generation industries like electric vehicles, wind turbines, solar panels, and high-efficiency electronics. A policy of hoarding and restricting exports of these materials ensures that domestic firms can move quickly to capitalize on emerging opportunities and maintain a strategic advantage over other nations.

While critics of resource nationalism highlight potential trade complications and diplomatic tensions, the urgency of protecting national security, fortifying economic well-being, and ensuring future stability strongly outweighs these concerns. By prioritizing domestic needs, hoarding key resources, and restricting or banning their export, the United States can minimize geopolitical vulnerabilities, foster homegrown innovation, preserve essential materials for future generations, and better weather unpredictable global disruptions. In an era defined by intense rivalries and accelerating technological shifts, strict resource nationalism represents a robust policy choice—one that will help guarantee American prosperity, sovereignty, and resilience in the decades ahead.
